Even though the ocean nearly took so much from them, the family of Coogee shark attack survivor Leah Stewart can still appreciate its wonders and rewards.

In a message read aloud to 1000 swimmers at Coogee Beach on Sunday, Stewart’s family encouraged them to look out for and wave to blue gropers, Leah’s favourite underwater sight, as they returned to the water en masse for the first time since the primary school teacher was attacked by a great white last weekend.

The 35-year-old mother remains in a critical condition at St Vincent’s Hospital. Surgeons have amputated one arm, and she faces a series of other serious procedures over coming days and weeks.

“Leah is a survivor,” her family said in a statement read by Coogee Surf Life Saving Club president Ben Heenan. “She draws her strength from the love and care she has surrounding her. It’ll be a long, painful, difficult road to recovery, but the support of her family, friends and community will help her as she fights to come back to the life and people she loves so deeply.”

Sunday’s fundraiser, designed to help ease the post-attack psychological tussle between the lure of the ocean and a fear of its most dangerous predators, was the sort of event Leah would have loved to be part of.

“This is the community Leah loved, and it’s amazing to see you all have her back,” her family said.

Nearly 30 paddleboarders, five boats, lifeguards and a drone patrolled the beach to help encourage swimmers back into the water. The heavy patrols provided much-needed reassurance, especially as word spread quickly that nearby Maroubra Beach had been temporarily closed earlier due to a shark sighting.

Camilla Martin, a Coogee regular, said Sunday’s swim was her first there since last weekend’s incident. “Statistically it’s super-rare, but attacks do happen,” she said.

“That’s mother nature out there, and it’s humbling. The more we can do to co-exist the better, but it can be scary. We all just have to figure our way through it.”

Paddleboard world champion Charlie Verco, who helped save Leah’s life after last Saturday’s attack, was repeatedly stopped by crowd members who thanked him for his bravery.

“I’ve spoken to lots of people who have felt a lot more resistance to getting in the water after this incident,” Verco told the Herald.

“But I think it is important to try and get back in the water. It’s such an important part of my lifestyle and if that was interrupted, the rest of my life would be changed and I don’t want that to happen. It provides me so much joy.

“You’re always aware of the risks, but this was such a freak incident that I don’t want it to change the way I feel about the water and my appreciation for how great the ocean is.”
